title: AF: anticoagulation at higher stroke risk
summary: Anticoagulation is recommended at annual thromboembolic risk ≥2%, exemplified by CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women.

title: AF: intermediate-risk anticoagulation discussion
summary: Anticoagulation is reasonable at annual thromboembolic risk 1% to <2%, corresponding to CHA₂DS₂-VASc 1 in men or 2 in women.
cautions: Risk modifiers and shared decisions matter.

title: AF: DOAC versus warfarin
summary: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for eligible AF anticoagulation candidates without mechanical valves or moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.
cautions: Review renal function, interactions and dosing.

title: Elective procedures: factor Xa inhibitor interruption
summary: Apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban: selected elective procedures use 1 full day off before low/moderate bleeding risk, or 2 before high risk.
population: When interruption is required; renal eligibility reviewed.
cautions: Also omit procedure-day doses. Urgent, neuraxial and severe-CKD pathways need separate review.

title: Dabigatran: interruption depends on CrCl
summary: Low/moderate versus high bleeding risk: CrCl ≥50 mL/min, 1 versus 2 days off; CrCl 30–<50, 2 versus 4 days.
cautions: Also omit procedure-day doses. CrCl <30, urgent and neuraxial pathways need separate review.

title: After procedures: DOAC resumption
summary: Resume after ≥24 hours for low/moderate bleeding risk or 48–72 hours for high risk, once hemostasis permits.

title: DVT/PE: primary-treatment duration
summary: ASH suggests 3–6 months of primary anticoagulation rather than 6–12 months. Most temporary-risk-factor VTE does not need continued secondary prevention afterward.
population: Adults with DVT/PE; cancer-specific guidance separate.
cautions: Recurrent events and persistent risk factors change duration decisions.

title: Unprovoked DVT/PE: extended prevention
summary: After primary treatment for unprovoked DVT/PE, indefinite antithrombotic therapy is suggested over stopping.
cautions: Does not apply to high bleeding risk; reassess benefit and harm regularly.

title: ACE inhibitor / ARB: kidney and potassium checks
summary: Check BP, creatinine and potassium within 2–4 weeks after initiation or dose increase; timing depends on GFR and potassium.
cautions: Earlier checks may be needed with instability or hyperkalemia risk.

title: HFrEF MRA: potassium and renal monitoring
summary: After MRA initiation or intensification, check potassium and renal function around 1 week, 4 weeks and every 6 months.
evidenceNote: Intervals are supportive text, not a separate graded recommendation.
cautions: Monitor more often with instability; eligibility and safety assessment remain necessary.

title: Lipid-lowering therapy: response monitoring
summary: Check a lipid profile 4–12 weeks after starting or adjusting therapy, then every 6–12 months to assess response and adherence.
cautions: Do not replace individual medication safety monitoring.

title: Metformin: vitamin B12 assessment
summary: Consider periodic B12 testing with long-term metformin, especially anemia or neuropathy. Supportive text advises annual testing after >4 years or with other deficiency risks.
evidenceNote: Grade B applies to periodic assessment; annual interval is supportive text.
cautions: Evaluate symptoms promptly rather than waiting for routine testing.

title: PPI: review indication and dose
summary: Regularly document the ongoing indication. Without a definitive chronic indication, consider a deprescribing trial; most long-term twice-daily users can be considered for once-daily dosing.

title: PPI: situations favoring continuation
summary: Generally avoid discontinuation with complicated GERD, Barrett’s esophagus, eosinophilic esophagitis, or high upper-GI bleeding risk.
cautions: Discuss transient rebound symptoms after withdrawal; review the full indication.

title: Benzodiazepines in older adults
summary: Generally taper benzodiazepines in adults aged ≥65 unless compelling reasons favor continuation, after individualized benefit–harm review.
evidenceNote: Clinical consensus, not an ACC/AHA evidence level.
cautions: Coordinate tapering and management of underlying conditions.

title: Benzodiazepine withdrawal: avoid abrupt cessation
summary: Do not abruptly stop when physical dependence is likely. A typical initial taper is 5–10% every 2–4 weeks, adjusted to symptoms.
population: Adults for whom benzodiazepine risks outweigh benefits.
evidenceNote: Individualized guidance; no separate grade extracted here.
cautions: Not an automatic taper prescription; severe withdrawal may require higher-level care.
